title: H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin
summary: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.
story_key: story|variant:image|title:h3 image day 0 support 4k in 0 87s with vera rubin
content_excerpt: We brought MiniMax H3-Image to NVIDIA Vera Rubin with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches 0.87 seconds median in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers 6,115 images/hour , projecting to 146,755 images/day . At USD 0.06879 per image , using MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue at full billable utilization, or USD 78.87/GPU/hour at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to consumer and data-center GPUs , spanning NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA) , as well as Huawei Ascend NPUs . Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated 4K image, resized to 1K and 2K with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. The two API modes are straightforward: Text-to-Image takes a prompt; Image Edit takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use 2K (2048×2048) and 4K (4096×4096) output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines. See MiniMax's API guide for the request parameters. Choose Text-to-image or Image Edit below. For editing, select 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 reference images ; output sizes reflect the measured cases. For 4K text-to-image , four GB300 GPUs average 1.48 seconds . A 4K image edit with one reference averages 1.77 seconds . A single RTX 5090 with CPU layerwise offload takes 52.29 seconds and 61.45 seconds for those same requests. Each timing includes the complete PNG response. For 2K text-to-image , a single H200 averages 1.49 seconds with BF16 and resident weights. For the detailed coffee-product prompt used here, Rubin averages 1.09 seconds at 4K. The 0.87-second headline comes from a separate short-prompt serving benchmark in Rubin Bringup , not this request. Both use four GPUs, SP4 and MXFP8; the request corpus, HTTP client and summary statistic differ. Every

title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
summary: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
summary: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
summary: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone tasks and relatively self-contained workflows in clean or curated workspaces. However, researchers ask agents to complete one step within an ongoing project, where requests depend on earlier session decisions and workspaces contain unfinished files, outdated versions, and failed attempts. We introduce ARE-bench to evaluate whether research agents advance ongoing projects while respecting prior decisions and existing workspace state, grounded in real session context and in-progress workspaces. ARE-bench includes 75 tasks built on agent sessions and full workspaces from recruited researchers' own projects, spanning seven research stages, 33 requirements, and 150 sub-requirements, with 1,173 binary checklist items in total. Each task is anchored at a real user request, preserves its requirements, and summarizes the earlier requests still in effect as background. The complete workspace is replayed to that boundary without cleanup, preserving artifacts from earlier turns. Each checklist is compiled from an intent-aligned rubric and credits any valid solution. Across seven frontier models, the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, and Design and Execution rank among the hardest stages for every model. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and material or workspace requirements are also checked. Evaluating delivery without these contextual requirements can therefore overestimate research agents and mask differences between them.

title: How Workday Built an Enterprise-Scale AI Agent Platform with LangGraph and LangSmith
summary: See how Workday used LangGraph and LangSmith to build an internal AI agent platform that cut prototype time from months to less than a day and compliance needs.
story_key: model:langgraph|title:how workday built an enterprise scale ai agent platform with langgraph and langs
content_excerpt: Workday is the trusted agentic platform for HR, finance, and IT, serving more than half the Fortune 500. The team set out to create the internal developer platform to build, deploy, and run AI agents in production, on Workday's infrastructure. The team leveraged LangGraph for agent orchestration and LangSmith for tracing, observability, and evals. In 2025, Workday’s leadership team saw the market opportunity for building agentic solutions and set an ambitious goal for agents in production by the end of 2026. Product teams needed a platform that could support both rapid prototyping and production deployments—a uniquely challenging mandate given Workday operates under some of the strictest security and data governance requirements in enterprise software. Getting any internal service into production means satisfying demanding audit, compliance, and data retention policies. The surface area was enormous for a team of four, encompassing a durable, scalable agent server; data access controls tied to Workday's audit policies; a collaborative eval platform; and an SDK that abstracted all of it. Workday’s Agent Platform team serves two user bases. 1.) the internal Workday engineering teams building agents, and 2.) the end customers of those agents. It lets teams focus on functional requirements, while handling authentication, security, compliance, and infrastructure. The first major product shipped was Workday's Agent System of Record, a governance layer that controls which APIs the agents are allowed to access. The Agent Platform team built the backend server and eval infrastructure that the system of record runs on top of. The team also built what Alex Gatto, Senior Machine Learning Engineer, describes as "Workday LangChain": a Python SDK that wraps LangChain primitives and routes them through Workday's internal services, including an LLM gateway, a RAG retrieval service, and other internal tooling. "Anytime there was some AI concept that LangChain had put out, we tried to build a Python SDK for that same concept, but at Workday," explained Alex. Workday chose LangGraph for agent orchestration to give internal developers maximum flexibility at the design layer, while providing standardized infrastructure underneath. title: Automating Design Quality in the Dark Factory
summary:
When agents build most of your screens, a designer reviewing everything at the end becomes the bottleneck. Hamza Oza, Lead Designer at Tessl, borrows from Toyota and his years as a mechanical engineer to build design quality into the line instead: redoing agent-built screens by hand to surface unwritten composition rules, turning them into brand and design skills, and adding advisory checks in CI, code review and weekly maintenance loops. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– What manufacturing teaches us about quality at scale
– Why a designer at the end of the line becomes a bottleneck
– Why design systems alone don't stop agents producing generic screens
– Surfacing unwritten composition rules by redoing agent work by hand

title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.

title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
summary: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.
